pages.description: \"Sperm cramps\" is not a medical diagnosis. Learn what may cause pain after ejaculation, why excessive Kegels can be unhelpful, and when to see a doctor.
h1: "Sperm Cramps": What Pain After Ejaculation May Actually Mean

headings.text: Prostatitis or Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome
What You Can Do While Arranging Care

pages.text: "Sperm cramps" is an informal internet term, not a recognized medical diagnosis. People usually use it to describe aching, pressure, cramping, or sharp pain during or after ejaculation. The discomfort may be felt in the penis, testicles, perineum, pelvis, groin, or lower abdomen. Sperm itself does not cramp. The symptom can involve the prostate, urinary or reproductive tract, pelvic floor muscles, nerves, or other nearby structures. Occasional mild discomfort may settle on its own, but repeated or severe pain should be evaluated rather than treated with random exercises. Common Symptoms People may describe: Burning or sharp pain during ejaculationA deep ache in the pelvis or perineumTesticular or groin discomfortCramping after orgasmPain when urinatingUrinary urgency or difficulty emptying the bladder The pattern, duration, and associated symptoms help a clinician narrow down the cause. Prostatitis or Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome Inflammation or pain associated with the prostate can cause discomfort in the perineum, penis, testicles, lower abdomen, or lower back. Some people also experience urinary symptoms or pain during or after ejaculation. Not every case is caused by a bacterial infection. Chronic pelvic pain syndrome can involve muscle tension, nerve sensitivity, stress, and other factors. Pelvic Floor Overactivity The pelvic floor contracts during ejaculation and then needs to relax. Research has found that some men with chronic pelvic pain—particularly those with ejaculation-related pain—have difficulty returning these muscles to a relaxed state. In this situation, repeatedly performing strong Kegels may increase tension. Treatment may focus on breathing, relaxation, manual therapy, coordination, and other techniques prescribed by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. See Can You Do Too Many Kegels? for more on overactive pelvic floors. Epididymitis or Other Infection Inflammation of the epididymis can cause testicular pain, tenderness, and swelling. Urinary tract infections and sexually transmitted infections can also contribute to genital or pelvic pain. These conditions require medical evaluation and may need prescription treatment. Exercises cannot eliminate an infection. Prostate or Pelvic Procedures Surgery, radiation, or other treatment involving the prostate or pelvis may change sensation, ejaculation, or muscle function. Tell your treating clinician about new pain rather than trying to rehabilitate the area without guidance. Hernia, Stones, or Other Conditions Groin hernias, urinary stones, nerve problems, and other conditions may produce pain that becomes noticeable during sexual activity. A physical examination may be necessary to distinguish them. Should You Do Kegels? Kegels can help when weakness or poor activation is the problem. They are not an automatic treatment for pelvic pain. If your pelvic floor is already tight, more contractions may increase pain or make relaxation more difficult. Do not begin an intensive strengthening program until a professional has assessed whether you need strengthening, relaxation, or both. What You Can Do While Arranging Care For mild symptoms without warning signs: Pause activities that clearly trigger painAvoid prolonged clenching of the pelvic floorUse slow diaphragmatic breathing and allow the lower abdomen to softenApply comfortable warmth to the pelvic areaRecord when the pain occurs and any urinary or sexual symptoms Over-the-counter pain medication may not be appropriate for everyone. Follow the label and ask a pharmacist or clinician if you take other medication, have kidney disease, ulcers, bleeding risk, or another relevant condition. Do not self-treat with leftover antibiotics. When to Contact a Doctor Arrange a medical assessment if pain is recurring, persistent, worsening, or affecting sexual activity. A primary-care clinician or urologist may ask about urinary symptoms, sexual history, medication, recent procedures, and possible infection. Seek urgent care for: Sudden severe testicular painSignificant swelling or rednessFever, chills, or vomitingBlood in urine or semenInability to urinatePain following a significant injury Final Thoughts Pain after ejaculation is real, but "sperm cramps" is too vague to explain its cause. Prostatitis, infection, pelvic floor overactivity, and other conditions can produce similar symptoms. The most important point is that pain does not always mean the pelvic floor is weak. Stronger Kegels may be the wrong solution when the muscles cannot relax. Persistent symptoms deserve proper evaluation and an individualized plan. This article provides general information and cannot diagnose the cause of pelvic or testicular pain. pages.title: Is Edging Bad for Testosterone?
pages.description: Edging is often blamed for lowering testosterone—or praised for boosting it. Learn what is actually known, the realistic benefits and risks, and how the pelvic floor may be affected.
h1: Is Edging Bad for Testosterone? What the Evidence Actually Says

headings.text: How to Practise Edging More Comfortably

pages.text: Edging means approaching orgasm and then reducing or stopping stimulation so that climax is delayed. A person may repeat this cycle during masturbation or partnered sex. Online claims describe edging as either a powerful testosterone booster or a cause of hormonal "exhaustion." Current evidence does not support either extreme. There is no good evidence that occasional edging causes a meaningful, lasting reduction in testosterone. There is also no convincing evidence that it creates a useful long-term testosterone increase. What Happens During Edging? Sexual arousal involves changes in blood flow, nervous-system activity, muscle tension, attention, and hormones. These responses naturally fluctuate throughout sexual activity. Short-term hormonal changes during arousal or abstinence should not be confused with a lasting improvement or decline in baseline testosterone. A diagnosis of low testosterone requires appropriate symptoms and properly timed blood testing—not an assumption based on sexual habits. Possible Benefits Some people use edging to: Learn how arousal buildsPractise delaying orgasmExtend a sexual experienceCommunicate preferences with a partnerExplore different rhythms and levels of stimulation These are subjective or skill-based benefits. They are not proof of hormonal enhancement. Temporary Aching or Pressure Prolonged arousal without orgasm may cause temporary genital heaviness or discomfort. This sensation is generally not dangerous and usually fades with time, reduced stimulation, or orgasm. No one is obligated to provide sexual activity to relieve another person's discomfort. Skin Irritation or Numbness Long sessions, high friction, strong vibration, or excessive pressure may irritate the skin or temporarily dull sensation. Use lubricant, change technique, and stop when discomfort begins. Persistent numbness, bruising, or pain requires medical advice. Pelvic Floor Tension Arousal and orgasm involve the pelvic floor. Repeatedly clenching these muscles for a long time may contribute to fatigue or tension in susceptible people. After a contraction, allow the pelvic floor to release fully. If edging causes pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, urinary urgency, or difficulty relaxing, take a break and consider evaluation by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. See Can You Do Too Many Kegels? for more on overactive pelvic floor symptoms. Performance Pressure Edging can become counterproductive if the person becomes preoccupied with timing, duration, or avoiding orgasm. Sexual activity should not feel like a test of discipline. If the practice causes anxiety, conflict, loss of sleep, soreness, or compulsive behaviour, reduce or stop it. Does Ejaculation Lower Testosterone? Research on ejaculation, abstinence, and testosterone is limited and often based on small studies. Temporary fluctuations have been reported, but they do not demonstrate that normal ejaculation lowers testosterone in a clinically meaningful way. Testosterone is influenced by many factors, including age, sleep, body composition, illness, medication, and testicular or pituitary function. Sexual frequency alone is not a reliable way to diagnose or manage low testosterone. How to Practise Edging More Comfortably Use sufficient lubricantReduce pressure and speed before discomfort appearsKeep sessions within a comfortable durationBreathe normally instead of bracing the abdomenAvoid continuous maximum-effort KegelsLet the pelvic floor soften during pausesCommunicate clearly with a partner and respect consentStop if you experience pain, numbness, or distress There is no medically required number of cycles and no health benefit to pushing through discomfort. How to Support Healthy Testosterone If your goal is general hormonal health, focus on factors with clearer evidence: Get adequate, consistent sleepPerform regular resistance and aerobic exerciseMaintain a sustainable body weightEat enough overall energy, protein, and dietary fatLimit excessive alcoholTreat sleep apnea and other medical conditionsDiscuss symptoms and testing with a healthcare professional Do not take testosterone or "testosterone boosters" without appropriate evaluation. Testosterone therapy has real indications, risks, and monitoring requirements. When to Seek Medical Advice Contact a clinician if you have persistent low libido, erectile difficulties, loss of morning erections, infertility concerns, testicular changes, unexplained fatigue, or other symptoms associated with low testosterone. Seek advice sooner if sexual activity causes recurrent pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, blood in urine or semen, or persistent numbness. Final Thoughts Edging is neither a proven testosterone hack nor a known cause of hormonal collapse. For most people, occasional edging is a matter of preference. The main concerns are comfort, irritation, pelvic floor tension, consent, and whether the practice begins to cause distress. Use it as an optional sexual technique—not as a hormone treatment. Only a qualified clinician can diagnose testosterone deficiency or the cause of persistent sexual symptoms. headings.text: Your Butt, Thighs or Abs Tighten
You Get a Headache, Back Pain or Stomach Ache
You Expect Results in a Week
A Correct Kegel in One Line

pages.text: Kegels look simple: squeeze, hold, release. But a lot of people do them in a way that does nothing—or even makes things worse. If you're wondering "am I doing Kegels wrong?", check these seven signs. You Hold Your Breath Sign: you realize at the end of a set that you haven't breathed. Fix: breathe normally the whole time. Try exhaling gently as you squeeze and inhaling as you release. Your Butt, Thighs or Abs Tighten Sign: you can see or feel your glutes clench or your belly pull in. Fix: put a hand on your stomach and one on your butt. Both should stay soft. Only the pelvic floor moves—an upward, inward lift. You Get a Headache, Back Pain or Stomach Ache Sign: discomfort anywhere after a session. Fix: Kegels shouldn't hurt. Pain usually means breath-holding or recruiting the wrong muscles. Go back to lying down, lower the intensity, and re-find the right muscles. You Never Fully Relax Sign: you rush from one squeeze to the next. Fix: the release matters as much as the squeeze. Relax for at least as long as you held—longer if needed. A muscle that can't relax isn't a healthy muscle. You Do Them While Peeing Sign: you use the toilet as your regular Kegel time. Fix: stopping your stream is only for identifying the muscles, at most once a month. Regular practice while urinating can disrupt normal bladder emptying. You Overdo It Sign: hundreds of reps a day, sore or tense feeling in the pelvis. Fix: more isn't better. A few sets of about 10 reps a day is plenty. Overtraining can leave the pelvic floor tight and tense instead of strong. See Can You Do Too Many Kegels? for more on this. You Expect Results in a Week Sign: you quit after 10 days because "nothing changed." Fix: most people notice changes after 6–8 weeks of regular practice. The first month is about learning control; visible results come later. Bonus: You Only Ever Squeeze Some people—especially men with a tense pelvic floor—also need reverse Kegels: deliberately relaxing and lengthening the same muscles. If you feel tight, have pelvic pain, or Kegels make symptoms worse, a pelvic floor physical therapist can tell you which one you need. A Correct Kegel in One Line Lift inward like you're holding in gas, breathe, hold 3 seconds, release fully 3 seconds—nothing else moves. h1: How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles (Men)

headings.text: What the Pelvic Floor Actually Is
Mistakes That Mean You're Squeezing the Wrong Muscles
Your First Kegel, Step by Step

pages.text: Before Kegels can do anything for you, you need to squeeze the right muscles. That sounds obvious, but it's where most men go wrong. Mayo Clinic Health System estimates that about 40% of people don't do a Kegel correctly on the first try. Here's how to find your pelvic floor muscles as a man, in a few minutes. What the Pelvic Floor Actually Is The pelvic floor is a group of muscles stretching from your pubic bone to your tailbone, like a hammock under your pelvis. It supports the bladder and bowel, and it plays a role in erections and ejaculation. You can't see it, which is why it's tricky to train. Method 1: The "Hold in Gas" Test Imagine you're in a quiet room and need to stop yourself from passing gas. The muscles you tighten to do that are your pelvic floor. This is the easiest and most reliable cue for most men. Method 2: The Mid-Stream Test (Once Only) While urinating, try to slow or stop the stream. The muscles that do this are part of the pelvic floor. Use this only to identify the muscles, and not more than about once a month. Doing Kegels while peeing regularly can interfere with normal bladder emptying. Method 3: The Perineum Check Lie on your back and place a finger on the perineum—the area between the scrotum and anus. Squeeze as if holding in gas. You should feel the area lift slightly upward and inward. Another visual cue: standing in front of a mirror, a correct squeeze makes the base of the penis pull in slightly and the testicles lift. Mistakes That Mean You're Squeezing the Wrong Muscles Clenching your butt. If your glutes tighten, you're compensating.Tightening your thighs. Legs stay relaxed.Sucking in your belly. Abs stay soft.Holding your breath. Breathe normally throughout.Pushing down instead of lifting up. A Kegel is an upward, inward lift. If you feel pain in your stomach, back or head afterward, that's usually a sign you're recruiting the wrong muscles or holding your breath. Your First Kegel, Step by Step Lie on your back, knees bent, fully relaxed.Squeeze the "hold in gas" muscles and lift inward.Hold for 3 seconds.Release completely for 3 seconds.Repeat 10 times. Once this feels easy lying down, try it sitting, then standing. When to See a Professional If you can't feel the muscles after a couple of weeks, or if Kegels cause pain, a pelvic floor physical therapist can help—often using biofeedback to show you exactly what you're contracting. pages.description: Most people quit Kegels because they forget, not because they don't work. 7 simple tricks to make a daily Kegel habit stick.
h1: How to Remember to Do Kegels Every Day

headings.text: Anchor Kegels to an Existing Habit
Use Reminders That Don't Feel Like Nagging
Do Them in a Set Position First, Then Anywhere
Don't Restart From Zero After a Missed Day

pages.text: Kegels work. The problem is that almost nobody keeps doing them. You start strong on Monday, forget by Thursday, and a month later you're back at zero. If you want to know how to remember to do Kegels, the answer isn't more willpower. It's building the habit into things you already do. Results usually show up after 6–8 weeks of consistent practice. That means consistency is the whole game. Here's how to make it automatic. Anchor Kegels to an Existing Habit Habit researchers call this "habit stacking": attach a new behavior to one you already do every day without thinking. Good anchors for Kegels: Waiting for coffee to brewRed lights while drivingBrushing your teeth (2 minutes = one full set)The first minute after you sit down at your deskEvery time you unlock your phone in the morning Pick one anchor, not five. One anchor you actually use beats a perfect plan you forget. Keep Sessions Tiny A set of 10 squeezes takes under two minutes. If your plan feels like a workout, you'll skip it. If it feels like nothing, you'll do it. Start with one short set a day and add more only after a full week without missing. Use Reminders That Don't Feel Like Nagging A phone alarm labeled "KEGELS" works for about three days, then you start swiping it away. Better options: A reminder with a neutral label only you understandA reminder tied to a location (arriving at the office)An app that turns the reminder into something you want to open Track Your Streak Seeing a chain of completed days is surprisingly motivating. Not wanting to break a 14-day streak is often what gets you through day 15. A calendar on the wall, a note on your phone, or an app—anything that shows the chain. Make It a Game Boredom kills Kegel routines faster than anything. Squeeze, hold, release, repeat—it's the same thing every day with nothing to show for it. Gamified training changes that. Instead of counting in your head, you're hitting targets, completing levels, or—in the case of Morse code training—spelling out words with short and long squeezes. Your brain stays engaged, and sessions stop feeling like a chore. See Kegel Exercise Games for more on why this works. Do Them in a Set Position First, Then Anywhere Most people find Kegels easiest lying down at first. Once you're confident you're squeezing the right muscles, move to sitting, then standing. When you can do them anywhere, your opportunities to practice multiply—and you'll forget less often. Don't Restart From Zero After a Missed Day Missing one day doesn't break your progress. Missing one day and then deciding "I'll start fresh next Monday" does. The rule: never miss twice in a row. pages.description: Always squeezing? Learn what reverse Kegels mean, how gentle breathing helps pelvic floor relaxation, and when men should seek a professional assessment.
h1: Reverse Kegels for Men: The Skill You Miss When You Only Squeeze

headings.text: What a Reverse Kegel Actually Means
Tight Does Not Automatically Mean Strong
When More Squeezing Is the Wrong Next Step

pages.text: You know how to squeeze. But can you actually let go afterward? If every pelvic floor session is about holding harder, the release can become an afterthought. Reverse Kegels are a common name for deliberately relaxing and lengthening the pelvic floor. They are not a competition to push downward. For some men, learning that distinction is more useful than adding another set. What a Reverse Kegel Actually Means A regular Kegel involves a lift and squeeze. Relaxation lets the muscles return from that contraction. The aim is comfortable movement, not a dramatic sensation or visible motion. Your breathing provides a useful cue: during an easy inhale, the diaphragm descends and the pelvic floor normally lengthens. Think of allowing that movement rather than forcing it. Plymouth's NHS relaxation guide describes this connection. Tight Does Not Automatically Mean Strong A pelvic floor that stays contracted may struggle to coordinate everyday functions. Pelvic discomfort, difficulty starting urine, constipation, or pain with ejaculation can occur with an overactive pelvic floor. They can also have other causes. That list is a reason to get assessed, not a home diagnostic test. Cleveland Clinic describes physical therapy as a central part of treatment for diagnosed hypertonicity. Try a Gentle Release Lie comfortably with knees bent and your head supported.Let your jaw, belly, and buttocks soften.Inhale slowly through your nose, allowing your abdomen and lower ribs to expand.Imagine the area underneath your pelvis becoming softer and less gripped.Exhale easily. Let the breath return without adding a deliberate squeeze. Try a few comfortable breaths. Do not hold your breath, bear down, or strain as though pushing out stool. Stop if this produces pain or worsens symptoms. When More Squeezing Is the Wrong Next Step If exercise brings on pain or leaves you feeling persistently clenched, pause the provoking routine and ask a pelvic health physiotherapist for help. They can assess both contraction and release. The 2025 AUA guideline recap discusses specialist physiotherapy for men with pelvic muscle pain, including approaches that reduce resting muscle tension. This is tailored care for assessed patients, not evidence that every man needs reverse Kegels. Should You Stop Regular Kegels? That depends on why you are training. Some people need strengthening; others need relaxation or a combination. A clinician can help decide when symptoms are present. For a technique refresher, see How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles. If your main concern is piling on repetitions, read Can You Do Too Many Kegels?. Where Guided Training Fits Kegel Morse Hero provides timing cues for squeeze-and-rest sessions. Use it when strengthening suits your plan; it cannot assess resting muscle tension or replace treatment for pelvic pain. pages.title: Dribbling After Peeing? Why That Last Drop Happens
pages.description: Finished peeing, then a few drops leak out? Learn why after-dribble happens, a gentle technique that may help, and where pelvic floor exercises fit.
h1: Dribbling After Peeing? Why That Last Drop Happens

headings.text: Why the Last Drop Waits Until You Move
The Mistake to Avoid: Training While Peeing
When It Is More Than After-Dribble

pages.text: You finish, wait, get dressed—and then a few drops escape. It is frustrating precisely because you thought you were done. This is often called post-micturition dribble, or after-dribble. It can happen at different ages. The useful question is whether those drops are left in the outlet tube or whether you are having a broader problem emptying your bladder. Why the Last Drop Waits Until You Move A small amount of urine can remain in the urethra, the tube carrying urine out of the body. Movement then lets it escape. Pelvic floor muscles help clear that tube, which explains why they can be part of the solution. The Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS guide explains this mechanism and a gentle clearing technique. A Technique to Ask About After urinating normally, wait a few seconds. With clean hands, place fingertips on the perineum, roughly three finger-widths behind the scrotum. Apply gentle pressure and move forward beneath the scrotum toward the base of the penis. Then clear the remaining drops normally. This is sometimes called urethral milking. It should not hurt or involve force. If you have recently had surgery, ask your care team before trying it. Where Kegels Can Help Pelvic floor training can help men with after-dribble, according to University Hospitals Sussex. First, learn a controlled inward lift with normal breathing and a clear release afterward. A continence nurse or physiotherapist can check the movement and suggest an appropriate routine. There is no reason to treat every toilet visit as an extra workout. Our guide to finding your pelvic floor muscles can help you understand the movement before practicing. The Mistake to Avoid: Training While Peeing Repeatedly stopping and starting the urine stream is not a daily Kegel routine. It can interfere with normal emptying. Practice separately, and let the pelvic floor relax while you urinate. If squeezing causes discomfort or you struggle to release, get advice before increasing repetitions. Pelvic floor relaxation is a different skill from squeezing harder. When It Is More Than After-Dribble Arrange an assessment if leakage comes with a weak stream, trouble getting started, or a repeated feeling that your bladder is not empty. Do not assume all leakage proves weak muscles. NIDDK explains that retention can also involve blockage, impaired bladder contraction, or tight pelvic floor muscles. If you cannot urinate, or have severe lower abdominal pain, seek urgent medical care. Make Training Easier to Follow If strengthening is appropriate for you, Kegel Morse Hero can guide squeeze-and-rest timing. It is a practice aid, not a test for the cause of leakage or a promise that symptoms will disappear. pages.title: Waking Up to Pee at Night: Can Kegels Help?
pages.description: Nightly bathroom trips are not always a weak pelvic floor. Learn possible causes of nocturia, what to track, and when Kegels may fit your care plan.
h1: Waking Up to Pee at Night? Kegels May Not Be the Answer

headings.text: When Pelvic Floor Training May Fit
Use a Training App for the Right Job

pages.text: Another bathroom trip. Another look at the ceiling while you try to fall asleep again. If this keeps happening, it is tempting to assume your pelvic floor needs more exercise. Waking from sleep to urinate is called nocturia. Kegels may belong in some bladder-care plans, but night waking alone does not tell you which treatment you need. One Symptom, Several Possible Causes Sometimes the body makes more urine during the night. Sometimes the bladder signals urgency at smaller volumes. Prostate-related emptying problems, certain medicines, and sleep disorders can also contribute. The Royal Devon NHS leaflet, issued in February 2025, separates nocturia from increased nighttime urine production. That distinction matters: stronger pelvic muscles do not directly switch off urine production. When Pelvic Floor Training May Fit For an overactive bladder, pelvic floor exercises may be used alongside bladder retraining to help manage urgency. Gateshead Health describes this approach. That does not establish Kegels as a universal nocturia treatment. If the problem is excess nighttime urine, an obstruction, or disrupted breathing during sleep, the underlying cause needs attention. Avoid inventing a nighttime schedule that forces you to hold urine through discomfort. Keep a Three-Day Record Before an appointment, write down: When and how much you drink.When you urinate and, if practical, the amount.Any urgency or leakage.Bedtime, waking time, and nighttime bathroom visits. NIDDK recommends a two-to-three-day bladder diary when investigating bladder control symptoms. Adding sleep times gives your clinician useful context for night waking. The record does not diagnose the cause. It makes the conversation more specific than “I go a lot.” Changes Worth Discussing Avoid large drinks close to bedtime and consider reducing evening caffeine or alcohol. Keep normal daytime hydration; do not deliberately dehydrate yourself to avoid the toilet. If you have a prescribed fluid limit, follow your clinician's instructions. Ask about medication timing rather than moving or stopping doses yourself. Don't Overlook Sleep Loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses, gasping, and marked daytime tiredness are reasons to ask about sleep apnoea. The NHS symptom guide explains what to look for. Night waking plus those symptoms deserves more than a stronger Kegel routine. When to Get Checked Book an appointment if repeated night trips disrupt sleep, especially with new urinary symptoms. If you cannot pass urine or have severe lower abdominal pain, seek urgent care; these can be signs of urinary retention. Use a Training App for the Right Job If pelvic floor strengthening is part of your plan, Kegel Morse Hero can help you follow squeeze-and-rest timing. It does not determine why you wake at night. For help keeping an appropriate routine consistent, read How to Remember to Do Kegels. pages.description: Not sure your Kegels are right? A step-by-step guide for men to finding the muscles, breathing, releasing fully, and checking technique before adding reps.
h1: How to Do Kegels Without Doing Them Wrong

headings.text: Step 3: Check What the Rest of Your Body Is Doing
Step 4: Build the Routine After the Movement

pages.text: You squeeze something, count to three, and hope it is the right muscle. Sound familiar? The tricky part of Kegels is that a lot of effort can feel convincing even when you are mostly clenching your butt or bracing your stomach. This guide walks men through a simple technique check. Start with one controlled repetition before worrying about a daily total. First, Check That Strengthening Fits If you already have pelvic pain, difficulty emptying your bladder, or symptoms that get worse with squeezing, get assessed before starting a strengthening routine. A pelvic floor can have trouble relaxing as well as contracting. Cleveland Clinic's guide to hypertonic pelvic floor explains why some people need treatment focused on restoring relaxation and coordination. Step 1: Find the Lift Lie on your back with your knees bent, or sit comfortably with your feet supported. Let your thighs and buttocks relax. Imagine stopping yourself from passing gas. Gently close around the back passage and draw the muscles inward and upward. Avoid pushing down as though trying to empty your bowels. In men, the base of the penis may move slightly toward the abdomen during a contraction. This is a possible cue, not a pass-or-fail test. University Hospitals Sussex describes the movement. If you are still unsure what you are feeling, see How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles. Step 2: Do One Complete Repetition Start in a comfortable position, with no deliberate squeeze.Lift the pelvic floor inward.Hold for about three seconds while breathing normally.Let the contraction go completely.Rest for about three seconds, or longer if you need time to release. This brief hold-and-rest pattern follows Mayo Clinic's beginner guidance. If you cannot maintain the hold without straining, shorten it. The goal is a controlled repetition, not winning a countdown. Step 3: Check What the Rest of Your Body Is Doing What you noticeWhat to tryYou stop breathingPause, return to easy breathing, and retry with less effort.Your buttocks clench or thighs squeeze togetherReset your position and focus on the small internal lift.You brace your belly hardReduce the effort; let your abdomen move naturally with breathing.You push downwardStop and return to the inward-lift cue. Get help if the direction remains unclear.You cannot feel yourself releaseRest longer instead of immediately adding another squeeze. These checks can highlight obvious mistakes, but they cannot confirm your technique as reliably as a professional assessment. Step 4: Build the Routine After the Movement Try a few comfortable repetitions first. Mayo Clinic describes gradually working toward 10 to 15 repetitions per set, with three sets a day. That is general guidance, not a target everyone must reach immediately. Your clinician may recommend a different hold, rest, or frequency. NIDDK advises an individual exercise plan and cautions against overdoing it. As control improves, practice sitting and standing too. Keep the same attention on breathing and release. Keep Toilet Time Separate Do not make stopping and restarting your urine stream a regular exercise. It can interfere with bladder emptying. The imagined “hold in gas” cue lets you practice away from the toilet. And do not keep a background squeeze going all day. Between repetitions and sessions, let the muscles rest. Still Unsure? Get Feedback If you cannot identify a clear lift and release, a pelvic floor physiotherapist can check what you are doing. Biofeedback may help you understand the contraction and relaxation. Stop exercises that cause pain or worsening symptoms. For further reading, see Am I Doing Kegels Wrong? and Reverse Kegels for Men. Let the App Handle Timing Once you know the movement and strengthening suits your plan, Kegel Morse Hero can guide squeeze-and-rest timing with Morse code patterns. It provides cues; it does not measure your contraction or verify which muscles you use.
